title: Vayelech: everyone gathers (Deuteronomy 31:10–13)
hookLine: every seven years men, women, children and strangers gather to hear the Torah

cards: Stadiums fill for games. Squares fill for marches and concerts. Almost nobody fills a stadium to hear someone read aloud.
Yet the Torah asks for exactly that crowd: one voice, a scroll, and thousands of people standing still to listen.
Men and women, toddlers on shoulders, foreigners who live in the land, all packed into one courtyard to hear words most of them already know. Moses commands it in Vayelech, once every seven years.

teach.h: ONCE IN SEVEN YEARS, AT SUKKOT.
teach.b: The command: at the end of every seventh year, the year of release, during the festival of Sukkot, the Torah is to be read before all Israel.
"Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn."
The word for assemble gives the ceremony its name: hakhel. Gather. The Mishnah, in Sotah, says the king himself read from Deuteronomy, on a wooden platform built in the Temple courtyard.

teach.h: AGRIPPA WEEPS: YOU ARE OUR BROTHER.
teach.b: King Agrippa received the scroll standing, though he was allowed to sit. When he reached the verse forbidding a foreigner as king, he wept, because his family came from outside.
And the people called out to him: don't be afraid, you are our brother. The Talmud asks a sharp question about the guest list. The men come to learn, the women come to hear.
But why bring the little ones? They won't understand a word. The answer: to give reward to those who bring them.
There's a plainer point in it too: a child who stands in that crowd once may remember the crowd, even without the words. Hakhel says learning isn't only private study.
Sometimes everyone needs to stand in one place, the king and the toddler and the stranger, and hear the same words together.
Since the Temple's destruction the ceremony hasn't been held in its old form, though some communities mark the year with gatherings of their own.

how: Hakhel was held at the Temple during Sukkot after each sabbatical year. Since the Temple's destruction it is not performed as commanded, but some communities and organizations in Israel and elsewhere hold commemorative public readings or gatherings in that year.

games.q: you're planning hakhel. a parent asks whether toddlers should stay home, since they won't understand a word. what does the Talmud say?
o: bring them: there's reward for those who bring them.
games.why: Chagigah 3a: the men to learn, the women to hear, and the little ones to give reward to those who bring them.

practice: Think of two or three people you could gather, family at dinner, friends on a call, coworkers at lunch, and one thing worth learning together: a short text, a grandparent's story, a question none of you can answer alone.
Picture everyone in one place, including someone who usually gets left out of these things.

wordCard.voice: Hakhel. Gather. The seven-yearly assembly where everyone, from king to child to stranger, hears the Torah together.

orig.note: Hebrew: assemble, gather. the command of Deuteronomy 31:12 and the name of the ceremony.

carryVoice: Your line: everyone gathers. The king, the toddler and the stranger, hearing the same words. See you tomorrow.
